edges.label: The topic 'Standard output and formatted printing' introduces formatted_output.
The topic 'Standard output and formatted printing' introduces standard_output.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Novices take output text literally, as if it acted on the program: printing "The value of X is 1" is read as setting X to 1. They also take 'print' to mean producing a finished line. In Java, print only appends characters to the output stream; it changes no variables and ends the line only for println.
[1] misconception (M) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: wrong rule: print and println behave the same (no newline difference). Right rule: println(s) prints s and then ends the line, but print(s) does not, so print("a"); print("b"); gives ab on one line.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: Points to LT (output appears in the order the output calls execute, with a line break only after println). An uneven trace drops a repeated value, puts output lines out of order, or adds line breaks after print on some calls. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
[3] misconception (M) -> PrintfAddsNewline: wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string to end the line.
[4] misconception (M) -> RepeatedOutputVariablePrintedOnce: wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once. Right rule: Every expression in the output is printed, so System.out.println(y + " " + x + " " + y) with x=6, y=9 prints 9 6 9.

[0] names_the_element (N): Standard output (System.out, StdOut) is the library abstraction for a program's text output: an output stream of characters written by print, println and printf.
[1] states_the_rule (S): print(s) writes s. println(s) writes s and then the line separator. println() only ends the line. A null String prints as "null". By default the stream goes to the terminal window.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): First the argument expression is evaluated, e.g. the concatenation "Sum is " + sum. Then its string form is appended, and println appends the line separator after it. Successive calls appear in execution order.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The output is the argument's string form. System.out.println(Math.PI) prints 3.141592653589793 (all digits), and println("Sum is " + 1778) prints Sum is 1778 followed by a newline. The methods return void.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One call appends text to the output (println also appends the line separator). It changes no variables and returns nothing.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each output call appends to the end of the single output stream, so the order of output is the order of execution.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): With `> file`, every print/println/printf writes to the file and nothing appears in the terminal. The program code is unchanged.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A prompt printed with print (not println) shows on the same line where the user then types, before the following StdIn read blocks. Output and input are separate streams.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): StdOut text and StdDraw pictures are independent outputs: printing does not draw, and drawing does not print.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): printf writes to the same stream as print and println, so mixed calls appear in call order. Unlike println, printf ends a line only when the format contains \n.
[5] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Standard output reports results (to a person, or to a file or program further down the line). Plan: an 'output' step after a computation, or one println per item inside a loop to list values.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: Switching System.out.print/println to StdOut.print/println keeps the output. Changing println to print keeps every character but removes the line break, so lines join.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use standard output for text results meant for a reader or for the next program in a pipeline. Use printf when digits or column widths matter, and StdDraw/StdAudio for pictures and sound.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Output order and line breaks follow the order of the calls and the print/println choice. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Output statements in the wrong order, or a missing println, so text fragments run together (e.g. the next prompt ends up on the same line).
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: PrintStream methods never throw IOException; a write failure only sets an internal flag. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Output to a closed or failing destination: nothing is reported unless checkError() is called.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: println/print take a single argument; pieces must be joined with +. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Calls like System.out.println("x =", x) with a comma-separated argument list: 'no suitable method found'.

StdIn takes values in from the input stream; StdOut sends values out to the output stream.
StdOut writes text to the output stream; StdDraw draws shapes at (x, y) coordinates in a window.
printf writes to standard output, like print, but formats each value first.
> file sends everything written to standard output into the file instead of the screen.
StdOut writes a stream: each print appends its text to the end of the output.
